title: What health and safety training does CCDF require for child care staff?
description: CCDF rules at 45 CFR 98.44: pre-service or orientation health and safety training within three months, the 11 required topics, and annual ongoing training.
shortAnswer: Under the Child Care and Development Block Grant Act and 45 CFR 98.44, each state, territory or tribe receiving CCDF funds must require caregivers, teachers and directors at subsidized providers to complete pre-service or orientation training, finished within three months, on 11 health and safety topics set out in 98.41, from safe sleep to pediatric first aid and CPR. Lead Agencies also name the topics required before unsupervised care and set minimum annual hours for ongoing training.
keyTakeaways: The federal rule sets the topics and structure; each Lead Agency (state, territory or tribe) sets the exact hours, delivery rules and which topics must be completed before a person cares for children unsupervised.
Pre-service or orientation training must be completed within three months and must cover the 11 topics in 45 CFR 98.41(a)(1)(i) to (xi), plus child development.
Ongoing professional development must include a minimum annual hours requirement set by the Lead Agency and must maintain and update the same health and safety topics.
The requirements reach every provider receiving CCDF assistance, including license-exempt providers, unless the Lead Agency exempts relative caregivers under 98.42(c).
As at November 2026, the May 2026 CCDF final rule did not amend 98.41 or 98.44; the training text dates from the September 30, 2016 final rule.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, implemented by each state, territory and tribe)
regulator: Office of Child Care, Administration for Children and Families (ACF), US Department of Health and Human Services
appliesTo: State, territorial and tribal Lead Agencies administering the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF)
Caregivers, teachers and directors of child care providers serving children who receive CCDF assistance, licensed or license-exempt
Training and professional development providers aligning courses with a Lead Agency's framework

sections.heading: How does the CCDF training requirement work?

blocks.text: It works through state plans. The [Child Care and Development Block Grant Act](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/9858c) at 42 U.S.C. 9858c(c)(2)(I) requires each state plan to certify that health and safety requirements are in effect, including "minimum health and safety training, to be completed pre-service or during an orientation period in addition to ongoing training". The implementing regulation, [45 CFR 98.44](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-98/subpart-E/section-98.44), tells the Lead Agency what its plan must describe.

The result is a federal floor of topics and timing, with the detail set locally. A child care center in one state may face a different number of orientation hours and a different list of before-unsupervised topics than a center across the border, but both lists must cover the same federal topics. This page describes the federal floor as at November 2026, from eCFR text current to November 5, 2026; check the CCDF plan and licensing rules of the state where care is provided.

sections.heading: Which health and safety topics must the training cover?

blocks.text: Eleven topics are mandatory and listed in [45 CFR 98.41(a)(1)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-98/subpart-E/section-98.41). Pre-service or orientation training under 98.44(b)(1)(i) must address each one:

items: Prevention and control of infectious diseases, including immunizations.
Prevention of sudden infant death syndrome and use of safe sleeping practices.
Administration of medication, consistent with standards for parental consent.
Prevention of and response to emergencies due to food and allergic reactions.
Building and physical premises safety, including identification of and protection from hazards, bodies of water and vehicular traffic.
Prevention of shaken baby syndrome, abusive head trauma and child maltreatment.

Emergency preparedness and response planning for natural disasters and man-caused events, including evacuation, relocation, shelter-in-place, lock down, staff and volunteer emergency preparedness training and practice drills, and reunification with families.
Handling and storage of hazardous materials and the appropriate disposal of biocontaminants.
Appropriate precautions in transporting children, if applicable.
Pediatric first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Recognition and reporting of child abuse and neglect.

blocks.text: At the Lead Agency's option, training may also cover the topics in 98.41(a)(1)(xii): nutrition including age-appropriate feeding, access to physical activity, caring for children with special needs, or any other subject the Lead Agency considers necessary. Orientation must also include child development across the major domains: cognitive, social, emotional, physical development and approaches to learning.

sections.heading: When must the training be completed?

blocks.text: Within three months, with some topics earlier. Section 98.44(b) requires the pre-service or orientation training to be completed within three months, and 98.44(b)(1)(i) requires the Lead Agency to specify the critical health and safety training that must be completed before caregivers, teachers and directors are allowed to care for children unsupervised.

That creates two clocks for every new hire: a short one for the critical topics before unsupervised work, and a three-month one for the full set. A provider's onboarding plan should show both, and supervision rosters should prevent a new staff member from being left alone with children until the critical topics are recorded as complete. See [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles) for a staged approach.

sections.heading: What ongoing training is required after orientation?

blocks.text: Ongoing, accessible professional development with a minimum annual hours requirement set by the Lead Agency. Under 98.44(b)(2) the ongoing training must:

items: Maintain and update the health and safety training standards in 98.41(a)(1)(i) to (xi), and the optional (xii) topics where adopted.
Incorporate knowledge and application of the state's early learning and developmental guidelines for children birth to kindergarten, where applicable.
Incorporate social-emotional behavior intervention models for children birth through school age, which may include positive behavior intervention and support and reducing expulsions and suspensions.
To the extent practicable, suit different age groups, English learners, children with developmental delays and disabilities, and Native American and Native Hawaiian children.
To the extent practicable, award continuing education units or be credit-bearing.

blocks.text: Because the hour count is set locally, the federal rule does not by itself fix an annual number. What it fixes is that health and safety knowledge is refreshed over time rather than taught once. For a method of choosing intervals, see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: Which providers are covered, and how is compliance checked?

blocks.text: All providers receiving CCDF assistance are covered, licensed or not. Under 98.41(c) the health and safety requirements apply to every provider of services paid for under the program, except relatives that a Lead Agency chooses to exclude under 98.42(c): grandparents, great grandparents, siblings living in a separate residence, aunts and uncles.

Compliance is checked through inspections under [45 CFR 98.42](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-98/subpart-E/section-98.42). Licensed providers must receive at least one pre-licensure inspection and at least one unannounced inspection a year covering health, safety and fire standards, and license-exempt CCDF providers must receive an annual inspection for health, safety and fire standards. Training records are among the first things an inspector can test against these standards.

sections.heading: Did the 2026 CCDF rule change training requirements?

blocks.text: No. The [Restoring Flexibility in the Child Care and Development Fund final rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/12/2026-09382/restoring-flexibility-in-the-child-care-and-development-fund-ccdf), published May 12, 2026 and effective July 13, 2026, rescinded the 7 percent family co-payment cap, the requirement to provide some direct services through grants or contracts, and the requirements to pay providers prospectively and based on enrollment. It did not amend 98.41 or 98.44, and the eCFR shows both sections unchanged since the September 30, 2016 final rule.

sections.heading: How can a provider map the CCDF rules to evidence?

blocks.text: A provider's file should prove three things for each staff member: what was completed before unsupervised care, that the full topic set was completed within three months, and that annual hours were met. The table below is an illustrative register; replace the bracketed items with the Lead Agency's own figures.

Head Start programs face an additional federal layer, covered in [Head Start staff training requirements](/regulations/head-start-staff-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats the 11 federal topics as a fixed framework and layers each state's hours and before-unsupervised list on top, so a multi-state operator can see where one course satisfies several states and where it does not. Each topic links to an assessment point and the evidence an inspector would ask for. See [public sector and grant-funded programs](/industries/government-defence).

faqs.q: How many hours of health and safety training does CCDF require?
faqs.a: The federal rule does not set a single number. 45 CFR 98.44 requires each Lead Agency to set the pre-service or orientation requirements, completed within three months, and a minimum annual hours requirement for ongoing professional development. The hours therefore come from the state, territory or tribe's CCDF plan and licensing rules.

faqs.q: Does CCDF training apply to license-exempt providers?
faqs.a: Yes, if they receive CCDF assistance. 98.41(c) applies the health and safety requirements to all providers of services paid for under the program, except relative caregivers that a Lead Agency chooses to exclude under 98.42(c). License-exempt CCDF providers also receive an annual health and safety inspection.

faqs.q: Can a new staff member work alone with children before finishing orientation?
faqs.a: Only once the critical topics the Lead Agency has specified are complete. 98.44(b)(1)(i) requires the Lead Agency to name the health and safety training that must be completed before caregivers, teachers and directors care for children unsupervised; the rest may be completed within the three-month window.

faqs.q: Is first aid and CPR training required for all child care staff?
faqs.a: Pediatric first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is one of the 11 mandatory topics in 98.41(a)(1)(x), so it must be covered in pre-service or orientation training and maintained through ongoing training. Renewal intervals and certification standards are set by state rules.
